NEW DELHI: Supreme Court 's order Sunday finding prima facie breach of its Oct 9 order against complete shutdown of Metro and train services and issuing notice to Union home secretary, Delhi Police commissioner and Delhi Metro chief altered over the course of a day senior advocate and Rajya Sabha MP Kapil Sibal 's views on the apex court.On Saturday, Sibal had told reporters "if we go to courts, I do not know whether we will ever get relief. The people of this country have decided that this govt has to go. If anyone can save the Constitution at this juncture, it is Supreme Court."He added, "I am tired of repeatedly approaching the SC. It's in my mind that there is no purpose in going there. I have not much expectations from SC. Whatever is to happen will happen. I only pray the country's democracy remains intact... The tribunals (in West Bengal) have allowed appeals of 93% voters whose names were deleted illegally. SC has come to know this. But we did not get any relief".On Sunday, he was leading a 100-strong team of lawyers in SC to question the detentions of protesters and alleged violations of court's Oct 9 order against shutdown of Metro and rail services. The emotionally charged arguments saw pro-protester lawyers paint a picture of injustice and violation of fundamental rights on Saturday, compare it to an "undeclared emergency" and shout down a senior advocate who said lawyers must confine their activities to courts and not hit the streets, and that freedom of speech came with reasonable restrictions.At an appropriate juncture, Justice Joymalya Bagchi said, "Our purpose is to instil people's faith in the system, and in that process your (lawyer's) confidence is most vital for our fight against injustice." The court also passed a slew of directives, including normalising Metro, train and internet services and traffic in the city and allowing lawyers and journalists to carry out professional work.Soon after the SC order, Sibal said, "We are deeply grateful to the Supreme Court for passing an order that restores the faith of the Indian people, as well as the faith of professionals, in the justice system of this country."Within an hour of SC passing the order, a senior advocate entered into an argument with cops over removal of barricades, citing the SC ruling. The order was yet to be made public and police personnel didn't know about it.
Article Summary: Supreme Court's order Sunday finding prima facie breach of its Oct 9 order against complete shutdown of Metro and train services. Rajya Sabha MP Kapil Sibal's views on the apex court altered over the course of a day. Sibal: "I am tired of repeatedly approaching the SC. It's in my mind that there is no purpose in going there"

Indian high commissioner to Canada, Dinesh Patnaik, has said India doesn't mind advocacy and protests for Khalistan, as long as these are peaceful. In an interview, Patnaik urged Canada to understand that activities around the separatist movement were taking place on its own soil, not in India."I have been saying from Day 1, Indians, Canadians, Sikhs can peacefully advocate for what they believe in, even if it is Khalistan or a separate homeland. Politically, we have zero problem," said Patnaik."In last 40 years, political parties in India have been advocating for that. So, it's nothing new... What we say... don't bring in negativity, filth, terrorist element, gun-running, organised crime and extortion into it.Don't have Khalistanis protesting with pictures of the killing of my PM," he said. The remarks came ahead of a Khalistan referendum scheduled for Alberta later this month.After a prolonged period of diplomatic strife over the killing of a Khalistani separatist in British Columbia in 2023, India and Canada have normalised the relationship and are currently discussing a potentially landmark trade deal. Both nations recently held another round of security dialogue, agreeing to deepen coordination in combating organised crime, terrorism and extremism.
Article Summary: Indian high commissioner to Canada, Dinesh Patnaik, has said India doesn't mind advocacy and protests for Khalistan, as long as these are peaceful. He urged Canada to understand that activities around the separatist movement were taking place on its own soil, not in India.

NEW DELHI: An IndiGo flight from Delhi to Chennai Sunday was diverted to Hyderabad after a passenger's personal electronic device caught fire. The crew put the device in water before the aircraft safely diverted to Hyderabad."6E 6115 was diverted to Hyderabad after smoke was detected from a customer's PED. Cabin crew responded promptly and the situation was brought under control. In line with established protocols, the pilots diverted the flight and landed safely at Hyderabad," an IndiGo spokesperson said.The personal electronic device (PED), containing a Li-ion battery, or power bank that caught fire was kept in overhead baggage.Many countries, including India, mandate that such devices be kept in front of passengers so they can quickly spot if they start emitting smoke or catch fire. We regret inconvenience caused to our customers due to this unforeseen situation and are making all efforts to minimise it, including offering refreshments and sharing updates. At IndiGo, safety of our customers and crew remains our top priority," the spokesperson added.

Article Title: How India travels: A tale of two wheels and many divides
Article Text:
File image of urban traffic

India on the move

Rural-urban divide

Two Indias, Two Ways to Travel

Students take the bus, workers take the bike

Men ride, women walk

The Gender Divide in India’s Commute

Short commutes, steeper city bills

City Travel Comes at a Price

The work clock

For long trips, the bus still rules

A quarter-century ago, an advertising campaign presented the two-wheeler as a symbol of “Naye Bharat ki Nayi Tasveer”. But is the India of 2026 still commuting mainly on two-wheelers, has it moved to cars, or are more people walking? The answer depends a great deal on which states people live in, whether they are in a village or a city, and on their gender. All three, in varying degrees, shape how people get around and how much they pay for it.Among some of the extremes featured in India’s National Household Travel Survey, in Puducherry, 92.7% of workers use a two-wheeler as their primary mode. In Nagaland, more than seven in ten walk. West Bengal has the highest published bicycle share, Ladakh stands out for buses, and Sikkim for cars. Conducted from July 2025 to June 2026, the survey covered 4,92,023 households and 18,44,179 people aged six and above.At the national level, the old two-wheeler image still rings true, though the averages hide big regional differences. Among workers who travel at least 1km to work, 42.6% mainly use a two-wheeler, 28.3% walk and 10.7% cycle. The average one-way trip to a fixed workplace takes 25 minutes, and travel costs about ₹785 a month per worker.Between India and Bharat, the numbers shift substantially. In rural India, workers are split almost evenly between two-wheelers at 37.1% and walking at 36.6%.In cities, the balance tips firmly towards the engine, presumably because of longer distances. Two-wheelers rise to 52.3% and walking falls to 13.5%. Autos, buses and cars all carry a bigger share too.The metro and local-train story is overwhelmingly urban. The survey’s Train/Monorail/Tram category, which includes metro rail and suburban or local trains, carries 5% of urban workers but just 0.4% of rural ones. In urban Maharashtra, home to Mumbai’s suburban railway, the share is 20.7%. It is 16.5% in urban West Bengal and 14.4% in Delhi, known for its metro network.The survey reports Rail separately. That category accounts for just 0.2% of workers nationally, 0.2% in rural India and 0.3% in urban India.Students and workers commute very differently. In villages, 40.5% of students walk and 18.9% cycle. In cities, buses at 33.7% and autos at 14.4% play a bigger role. Nationally, 37% of students walk, 29.5% take a bus and 15.8% cycle, while only 6.7% use a two-wheeler. Among workers, buses account for just 6.7%, exactly the share two-wheelers have among students.The contrast is sharpest in Kerala, where buses carry 72% of students but 24.9% of workers. Age changes the picture too. Students aged 15 to 29 walk far less than those aged 6 to 14, 22.2% against 47.3%, and cycle more, 21.4% against 11.9%.Among workers, 47.1% of men use a two-wheeler to get to work. Among women, it is 18.4%. About half of female workers, 50.6%, walk, against 24.1% of men. Women are also much more likely to take the bus, 14% against 5.3%.It would be easy to put this down to rural India, where more people walk. But the divide holds in cities too. There, 57% of male workers use two-wheelers, against 25.8% of women, while women are twice as likely as men to walk, 24% against 11.6%. The bicycle divide is even starker in relative terms. Among workers, 12.3% of men cycle to work but only 1.7% of women do.Yet among students, the sexes are much closer. Some 17.7% of male students cycle, against 13.4% of female students. Odisha makes the contrast particularly striking. Female students there cycle almost as often as male students, 32.8% against 34%. Among workers, though, the Odisha gap opens up. Some 25.5% of men cycle to work, against 5.8% of women.Most work commutes are under half an hour. Some 83.4% of workers travelling to a fixed workplace get there within 30 minutes. Students do even better, with 87.6% reaching school or college within half an hour.However, travelling in cities is much costlier. The average urban trip to work takes 27 minutes, just four more than in villages, but costs ₹1,044 a month against ₹612, about 71% more. Urban students pay about 71% more too, even though their average trip is a shade shorter, 22 minutes against 23 in villages.Even within cities, there are stark differences. Workers in urban West Bengal and urban Delhi spend about the same time getting to work, 36 and 35 minutes on average. But the urban West Bengal worker spends about ₹825 a month, while the urban Delhi worker spends about ₹2,081, roughly two and a half times as much.Urban West Bengal also has a much bigger long-commute tail. Some 13% need over an hour to commute, against 4.1% across urban India. Hence, lower monthly spending there does not necessarily mean a quicker journey.Across India, 56.5% leave for work between 8am and 10am. In Mizoram and Ladakh, some 97.1% and 95.1% of commuters leave between 8am and 10am.Evenings vary even more. Across India, 31.1% leave work at 6pm or later. In Tamil Nadu it is nearly half, 48.9%, with Gujarat at 45.2% and Delhi at 44.6%. Men are more than twice as likely as women to be leaving that late, 34.1% against 16%.Take work and study out of the picture and far fewer people step out at all. On a given day, 18.7% of people aged six and above travelled at least 1km for some other reason, 23.8% of males and 13.3% of females.They also get there differently. Among men making such trips, 40.1% use a two-wheeler, against 17.6% of women. Among women, 30.4% take an auto or e-rickshaw, against 12.7% of men. For women, autos and e-rickshaws play much the same role that two-wheelers do for men.In the 28 travel days before the survey, 11.3% of households made an overnight trip of 50km or more that kept a member away from home for more than 24 hours. More than half of these households, 55.8%, used the bus as their primary mode.The separately reported Rail category comes next at 17.7%. Cars account for 15.1% and two-wheelers 8.8%. Another 3.3% fall under Train/Monorail/Tram. Just 0.6% travelled by air.Few of these trips were about work. Some 70.2% of households making overnight trips travelled for socialising, communication or religious purposes.How far are people travelling? The answer is not provided in the details released so far. The survey collected trip distances, as well as information on licences, household vehicles and bus or rail passes, but none of these appears in the released estimate tables.A quarter-century after the “Naya Bharat” pitch, the two-wheeler still leads the national picture. But the survey shows how much that picture hides, and the big missing piece is how far India travels. At a time when there is demand for metros in every Tier 2 city and road and rail connectivity is better than ever, the full data, when released, will help policymakers make more informed decisions about how to prioritise India’s transport needs.
Article Summary: In Puducherry, 92.7% of workers use a two-wheeler as their primary mode. In Nagaland, more than seven in ten walk. West Bengal has the highest published bicycle share. Ladakh stands out for buses, and Sikkim for cars.

Article Title: Don't detain peaceful protesters, says SC; hundreds still taken away on Day 2
Article Text:
Normalise internet connectivity, ensure free movement in city: SC

NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Sunday sought responses of Union home secretary Govind Mohan, Delhi police commissioner Anurag Kumar and Delhi metro rail chief D Thara to a contempt petition for prima facie violating the court's Oct 9 order against complete shutdown of metro and train services in Delhi on Saturday to thwart CJP's protest seeking CEC Gyanesh Kumar's resignation. The court also said lawyers, journalists, and other professionals should not be hindered in performing their duties "in any manner whatsoever".On the ground, nearly 700 people were detained (police claimed 400), many far away from protest zones, while barricading and traffic curbs remained on the roads much like Saturday. Protesters changed strategy, staging flash protests in small numbers at short notice. Most of the action was in and around CP as small groups of protesters kept trickling in. They were detained.Around 2.30pm, All India Student Association members, including president Neha Bora, started a protest near RK Ashram Marg metro station. As detentions began, Bora and a few others broke away and ran towards CP, where they continued to protest before being detained. Around 7pm, Students Federation of India members gathered at CP to hold a women's tiranga march against alleged police excesses, especially against women protesters.They were detained and taken away in buses. "How can they detain women at 7pm in the evening?" SFI general secretary Srijan Bhattacharya said.The widespread detentions - 7,000 estimated Saturday - figured prominently in arguments by the lawyers at SC's unusual holiday hearing on Sunday. Following the submissions, a bench of Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said, "...we are of the opinion that the petitioners have made out a prima facie case. Accordingly, we issue notice upon the alleged contemnors". It asked them to file their responses by Oct 13.We understand the gargantuan magnitude of detentions. We will have to seek a response from govt," the bench said after hearing the petitioners, who included advocate Shailendra Mani Tripathi, CPM MP M A Baby, RJD MP Manoj Jha and lawyer intervenors like Shadan Farasat, who was detained along with other advocates outside SC on Saturday.The bench asked for normalisation of internet connectivity and prohibition of "illegal" detentions, especially of those who gather for peaceful protest away from areas where prohibitory orders are in force. "There shall be no illegal detentions, particularly in cases of peaceful unarmed assemblage of people beyond the area where prohibitory orders under Sec 163 of BNS are in force," it said.On Oct 9, SC had restrained authorities from resorting to blanket closure of metro stations, though it said operations could be regulated depending on the situation. The order came after DMRC said 57 stations would be shut; that number was later revised to 45.Solicitor general Tushar Mehta disputed allegations of violation of the Oct 9 order and said Delhi Metro was functioning normally, though 45 out of 303 stations were closed to maintain law and order. He refuted the allegation that metro stations were closed, saying that "all metro stations are open since 10pm Saturday, trains are operating normally and internet connection has been restored".SC also issued directions to ensure free movement in the city subject to law and order situation/traffic regulations and that installing barricades shall be reviewed forthwith to ensure free movement subject to law and order and traffic requirements. "Lawyers, journalists and other professionals shall not be hindered in discharge of their professional duties in any manner whatsoever," SC said, and also directed withdrawal of prohibitory orders around SC and courts to facilitate free access to litigants and lawyers.Over 100 lawyers led by senior advocate and MP Kapil Sibal slammed the police brutalities on protesters, and accused authorities of continuing with the shutdown of metro and train services in complete disregard of the SC order and of illegal detention of protesters even in areas where the prohibitory orders were not in force.Sibal argued that internet shutdown was a blow to fundamental right to free speech and flagged detention of lawyers who participated in the protest. Senior advocate Farasat, who was detained, informed SC he was manhandled and bundled into a police vehicle. Senior advocate and TMC MP Menaka Guruswamy termed the entire episode as "undeclared emergency" worse than what Indira Gandhi had imposed (in 1975).When Sibal thanked the bench for holding court on Sunday because of the extraordinary turn of events, Justice Bagchi said, "We are always at the service of the nation." Later, Justice Bagchi said, "We know things have deeply affected you (the lawyers) and we do not want to trivialise anything."The bench issued notice to Centre and Delhi Police on a habeas corpus petition questioning detention of TMC politicians Mamata Banerjee, Derek O'Brien and Dola Sen. Solicitor general Mehta said the petition has become infructuous as the detained leaders were released last evening.As the pro-protest petitioners backed by a team of senior advocates - K K Venugopal, N Hariharan, Shoeb Alam, Arundhati Katju, G Sankaranarayanan, Sanjay Hegde - made a concerted attempt to corner police and Centre by flagging police action, senior advocate Kirti Uppal struck a discordant note by arguing that lawyers should not be stepping into shoes of their political affiliation."I was told that a lawyer's job is inside the courts and not on the streets," he said. The pro-protester lawyers inside the courtroom shouted 'shame, shame' to silence him. The bench asked the lawyers to maintain decorum of the courtroom and maintain silence.
Article Summary: Supreme Court Sunday sought responses of Union home secretary Govind Mohan, Delhi police commissioner Anurag Kumar and Delhi metro rail chief D Thara to a contempt petition. Nearly 700 people were detained (police claimed 400), many far away from protest zones. Protesters changed strategy, staging flash protests in small numbers at short notice.

Article Title: 'Supreme Court's doors are open to everyone': CJI Surya Kant after declining to meet INDIA bloc leaders
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: The Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant on Monday said the Supreme Court’s doors were open to everyone, a day after declining to meet INDIA bloc leaders seeking to discuss concerns over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.“I received a letter yesterday regarding a meeting request, and I responded to it last night, outlining the reasons why I will be unable to meet...” he said.Whe asked what reasons he has citied, he said, "Please don't ask me about that. I have maintained the confidentiality of that." "We will not allow SC to become a political battle field, the CJI said possibly reacting to the Opposition's decision to take out a march to SC. "Wherever designated plcaes are, the protest can be held there in accordance with law," the CJI added further.While talking to reporters, he further added that any common citizen or elected representative could approach the court, and their concerns would be heard and relief granted in accordance with the law."Any petition from any common citizen or member of an elected body is welcome. Every Indian citizen has the right to approach the court, and we will hear their concerns and grant whatever is due under the law."On Sunday, Lok Sabha LoP Rahul Gandhi announced that the opposition parties would march to the Supreme Court on Monday and will present a memorandum to the CJI seeking the rollback of the SIR and resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar.Mallikarjun Kharge also announced the same plan, and stated that they have scheduled a meeting with the CJI between 4 PM and 5PM tomorrow.
Article Summary: Chief Justice of India Surya Kant on Monday said the Supreme Court’s doors were open to everyone, a day after declining to meet INDIA bloc leaders seeking to discuss concerns over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. "We will not allow SC to become a political battle field," the CJI said.

Article Text:

NEW DELHI: Amid the clampdown in Delhi, Indian govt for the second time in two days slammed Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) for raising concerns about mass detentions in the city, saying this constituted an unacceptable interference in India's internal affairs.While Indian mission to UN in Geneva said Saturday Indian citizens exercise their right to peaceful assembly subject to "reasonable restrictions" in the interest of public order, the ministry of external affairs tweaked the phrasing to "maintenance of public order and safety".Govt also accused the UN human rights office of practising double standards, alluding to the crackdown in PoK, saying this erodes the credibility of its standing and contributes to loss of faith in multilateralism."We also note OHCHR has an approach of extreme selectivity when it comes to public positions. Violent responses to protests in our neighbourhood have gone uncommented, as indeed have law enforcement actions in its own vicinity," said MEA, also referring to action in countries like France, Belgium and Germany without naming them.The UN body had urged Indian authorities to release all those detained.The MEA said India is the world's largest democracy, where the right to peaceful assembly is guaranteed by Constitution and safeguarded by robust institutions, an independent judiciary and a free media."As in every democracy, Indian citizens exercise this right subject to the maintenance of public order... Our law enforcement authorities act strictly in accordance with the law, and our courts remain available to all for the redressal of any grievances," it said, adding OHCHR's concerns were unwarranted.
Article Summary: Indian govt for the second time in two days slammed Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) for raising concerns about mass detentions in Delhi. Indian mission to UN in Geneva said Saturday Indian citizens exercise their right to peaceful assembly subject to "reasonable restrictions" in the interest of public order.

NEW DELHI: Police visited Trinamool Congress (TMC) national general secretary Abhishek Banerjee 's residence in Kolkata on Sunday. They served a notice summoning him for another round of questioning in connection with the Camac Street party office billboard case, an officer said. This was the police's second visit to his Kalighat residence in a week to serve the notice.A team from Shakespeare Sarani police station reached the Diamond Harbour MP's residence to deliver the notice. The move followed a complaint lodged by the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC). The civic body alleged that police personnel and civic workers were harassed and assaulted while trying to remove TMC signage from a building on Camac Street that houses a party office.Police had visited Banerjee's residence on October 7 for the same purpose. However, he was not at home at the time. No one was available to receive the notice, the officer said.On Sunday, the situation was initially similar. No one was ready to accept the notice when the police team arrived. After some time, however, the notice was handed over to Banerjee's staff at the residence, the officer said.The case relates to a disturbance on August 27. Police and KMC officials had attempted to remove a billboard bearing the TMC name and its twin-flower symbol from the building housing Banerjee's office on Camac Street in central Kolkata.The action triggered protests by Banerjee's supporters, who opposed the removal of the signage.Three FIRs were registered at Shakespeare Sarani police station in connection with the incident. Banerjee has already been questioned in one of the cases. He appeared at the police station and spoke to investigators for several hours. Police now want to question him again in the same case.The fire department had also separately served a notice in connection with the matter.Meanwhile, TMC spokesperson and MLA Kunal Ghosh criticised the police action. He objected to the timing of the notice, with Durga Puja just days away. Condemning the move, Ghosh said, "The BJP (government) has stooped so low that a notice has been served even after Mahalaya when the Durga Puja is just days away."
Article Summary: Police visited Abhishek Banerjee's residence in Kolkata on Sunday. They served a notice summoning him for another round of questioning. This was the police's second visit to his Kalighat residence in a week to serve the notice. The case relates to a disturbance on August 27.

Article Title: Presidential election today? Trump confuses India with Brazil, claims 125 million voted

US President Donald Trump on Monday confused India with Brazil, claiming that 125 million people had voted in an Indian “presidential election”, while also questioning the integrity of the American voting system.In a post on Truth Social, Trump wrote, “125 Million People voted today in the first round of India’s Presidential Election. The results came out shortly after the vote closed, on the same day!”He then compared the alleged election results with the US electoral process, writing, “In Detroit, Philadelphia, California, and numerous other US Cities and States, the results, with much smaller numbers, will often take weeks to Rig, I mean, calculate. Voting in America is corrupt!!!”However, India did not hold a presidential election on Sunday. The President of India is elected indirectly by an electoral college and not through a direct nationwide popular vote.Trump's remarks came after Brazil held the first round of its presidential election on Sunday, with incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro advancing to the October 25 runoff.With 99.99% of the votes counted, Bolsonaro secured 47.03% of the valid votes, while Lula received 45.16%, according to Brazil's Superior Electoral Court.The figure of around 125 million mentioned by Trump is close to Brazil's total valid votes, which stood at about 125.27 million, suggesting he may have confused the Brazilian election with India.Neither Bolsonaro nor Lula crossed the 50% threshold required to win in the first round, triggering the October 25 runoff, BBC reported.Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro, outperformed expectations in the first round and finished ahead of Lula. His strong showing has raised the prospect of a shift to the right in Latin America's largest economy.Brazil has used electronic voting for decades, and electoral authorities said the first-round voting process proceeded smoothly.The Organization of American States' electoral observation mission said “the voting has been going smoothly and under adequate safety conditions.”The rapid announcement of results has also been cited as a strength of Brazil's electronic voting system.“When results take a lot of time, it creates an opening for people to cast doubt on the results, to say there’s been a problem,” Josemar Lauriano Pereira, a 46-year-old lawyer in Rio de Janeiro, told the Associated Press.Trump's post drew reactions on social media, with users pointing out that India does not elect its president through a direct popular vote.One user posted, “Trump living in a different world? Is a presidential election taking place in India? President Donald Trump made the incorrect claim that 125 million people voted in India's "presidential election" today.”Another said, “What is my blud Donald Trump smoking? Why is he mentioning India instead of Brazil when talking about the election?”

Article Title: SIR strikes at heart of Constitution: Supreme Court judge Ujjal Bhuyan
Article Text:
File photo: Supreme Court of India Judge Justice Ujjal Bhuyan (PTI Photo)

-

Detaching right to vote from citizen is like taking soul out of body: Bhuyan

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Launching a scathing attack on special intensive revision (SIR) that has resulted in large-scale deletion of names from voter lists across states, Supreme Court judge Justice Ujjal Bhuyan on Sunday said any process disenfranchising millions of Indian citizens was intrinsically arbitrary as it struck at the heart of the Constitution.Discounting the reasons given by govt and EC to justify SIR, which was upheld in the case of the revision of rolls in West Bengal by SC with modifications, Justice Bhuyan said, "No amount of whataboutery can justify it. It strikes at the very heart of Constitution. I would go to the extent of saying that it is a negation of the constitutional order which we have adopted under the Constitution."He was speaking at the moot court valedictory function at Nalsar, Hyderabad.Nalsar students, who had opposed CJI Surya Kant's participation in the convocation ceremony recently, came in for praise from Justice Bhuyan.Also read| Democracy in peril as voters illegally ousted: Former SC judge Justice Rohinton Fali Nariman "One last word about the brilliant students of Nalsar. You have shown to the country and to the world what a university student, that too a student of law, should be. You are brilliant, you are bold, and you are brave," he said.Justice Bhuyan said a citizen’s right to vote was central to the holding of free and fair elections.“Except in the case of a dead voter, the name of a voter once enlisted in the electoral roll cannot be deleted without notice and hearing,” he added.The SC judge said the right to vote or be included in the voters’ list could not be detached from the persona of an Indian citizen.Also read: EC orders special drive to add genuine electors 'left out' during SIR “If it is done, it will be like taking out the soul from the body,” he added. Justice Bhuyan said the Indian Constitution does not provide for two classes of citizens: citizens with voting rights and citizens without voting rights. “Any process which leads to wholesale disenfranchisement of Indian citizens, making them citizens without voting rights, would be violative of Articles 326 and 14 of Constitution of India,” he said.“If any process results in disenfranchising millions and millions of Indian citizens, making them second class citizens in their own country in the sense of being citizens without voting rights, such a process is intrinsically arbitrary,” he added, his remarks coinciding with attacks on EC and govt over SIR by the opposition and others.Justice Bhuyan said the right to vote was intertwined with India’s years of struggle against foreign rule. “It is a manifestation of our freedom achieved after so much struggle and sacrifice. Article 326 (universal adult franchise) cannot be tinkered with at all. No authority can do it, no court can condone it. No one is above Constitution,” he said.
Article Summary: Supreme Court judge Justice Ujjal Bhuyan said any process disenfranchising millions of Indian citizens was intrinsically arbitrary as it struck at the heart of the Constitution. He was speaking at the moot court valedictory function at Nalsar, Hyderabad. “If it is done, it will be like taking out the soul from the body,” he added.

Abhishek Sharma continues to redefine aggressive batting in T20 Internationals, combining an extraordinary scoring rate with the ability to find solutions when opposition bowlers try to expose his weaknesses. The India opener crossed the 2,000-run mark in T20Is during the third match against West Indies in Indore on Sunday, and former India batter Ajinkya Rahane believes his ability to adapt without compromising his attacking intent makes him a special talent.Abhishek smashed 69 off just 30 deliveries to power India to a formidable total of 223 in the third T20I, helping the hosts take a 2-1 lead in the five-match series. His innings featured explosive strokeplay, but Rahane was particularly impressed by the left-hander's approach against off-spinner Roston Chase, an area in which Abhishek has faced challenges previously.Speaking on Cricbuzz, Rahane praised the youngster's ability to find different methods of scoring runs while maintaining his trademark aggression and high strike rate."See, he's a special talent. We were talking about him, his intent every single time.What I like about Abhishek Sharma is his finding methods to score runs. If he's struggling with a particular area, he will find a way, find that different method to score runs without losing that intent, without losing that strike rate, I mean," Rahane said.Abhishek's approach against Chase in Indore offered a glimpse of the adaptability Rahane highlighted. Rather than immediately taking on the off-spinner, the left-hander initially played a few deliveries cautiously before switching gears in the third over, striking two sixes and a boundary through the off-side.The adjustment allowed Abhishek to counter the challenge without abandoning his natural attacking instincts, underlining why Rahane considers his batting approach particularly impressive. Abhishek boasts a T20I strike rate of 195.95, the highest among batters who have faced at least 250 deliveries in the format.Rahane also highlighted the remarkable consistency behind the opener's aggressive style, pointing to his ability to maintain a scoring rate close to 200 across his international career."We see his strike rate throughout his career so far is close to 200. And the consistency is so amazing. (He is) the fastest player or batter to score 2000 runs in T20 format, which is something amazing," Rahane added.The third T20I against West Indies marked another significant milestone in Abhishek's rapidly growing international career. He became the fastest batter to reach 2,000 T20I runs in terms of balls faced, taking just 1,024 deliveries to reach the landmark.Abhishek is currently ranked No. 2 in the ICC men's T20I batting rankings, having previously occupied the top spot.He also continued his remarkable six-hitting run in 2026. His 69-run knock against West Indies took his tally to 68 sixes in the calendar year, equalling Suryakumar Yadav's record for the most sixes by a batter from a Full Member nation in men's T20Is in a calendar year.

NEW DELHI: India’s bowlers had a clear plan to stop Shai Hope ’s impressive run against them, and left-arm pacer Arshdeep Singh was delighted to see it work in the third T20I against the West Indies in Indore on Sunday.Hope had been in sensational form across the ODI and T20I series, scoring back-to-back centuries in the 50-over format before producing a half-century in the opening T20I and an unbeaten 102 in the second. But the West Indies captain managed just five runs in Indore, bowled by Arshdeep in the second over as India restricted the visitors to 209/7 while defending 223.India won by 14 runs to take a 2-1 lead in the five-match series, with Arshdeep finishing with three wickets, including the crucial dismissals of Hope, Sherfane Rutherford and Keemo Paul.“Before the match, we had planned how to keep things tight to him and when you execute that plan in the match, it feels good when you get the result. I am grateful to the coaches for working through the plan and they told me that I can use this in the match and that thing got executed,” Arshdeep said in a video posted on bcci.tv on Monday.Arshdeep credited the entire bowling attack for maintaining pressure while defending a formidable total, pointing to the collective effort that helped India bounce back after West Indies chased down 250 in the previous match.“I bowled very well. Mayank kept the pressure from the other end and all the six bowlers, all chipped in and bowled very well. It feels good when you get a little pressure for executing plans. So, it's good fun,” he said.Arshdeep also had a light-hearted moment when he apologised to Axar Patel for the mid-pitch mix-up that resulted in the all-rounder's run-out.“I would like to apologise to Axar bhai. Sorry, Axar bhai. I got you run out,” he said.The pacer said he continues to work on his batting, too, as India look for useful contributions from the lower order.“I keep trying in batting. The results are rare. But today, it just connected well. As much as the coaches trust us, we have to do it in batting as well and get a few runs down the order. So it is important to work like this in batting,” he added.Former West Indies pacer Ian Bishop also credited India’s execution, highlighting their use of yorkers and wide lines, Arshdeep’s leadership of the attack and Naman Dhir’s support. He also pointed to the absence of dew as a factor that helped the bowlers."First of all, congratulations to India. The West Indies found a little bit of range with the ball after about over number eight through Roston Chase, then Springer, then Motie, but those runs at the back end by Prince Yadav proved crucial. Then we saw the yorkers. Shreyas Iyer mentioned at the toss that he brought Prince Yadav back into the team for the first time in the series so they could get guys bowling those yorkers and wide lines, and those are critical plans."Arshdeep is the leader of the attack, and he sussed things out quite quickly, with a little bit of help from Naman Dhir. A critical factor, obviously, was that there was no dew formation. All in all, it’s good to see the bowlers having a better day in a batsman-dominated series so far. The West Indies will look to do a few things better next time, but take nothing away from India; they deserved this win from a bowling perspective,” Bishop told JioStar.Arshdeep, meanwhile, said the relaxed atmosphere in the Indian dressing room and his willingness to learn continue to help him improve.“In the dressing room, the environment is very chill. There is no one who behaves as if they have played more or less matches. The atmosphere is very chill,” he said.“I keep trying to learn about something and get in a different skill set. There is always that willingness to learn and improve my game and I feel if there is a hunger to learn, then I will keep improving my game and I keep trying that,” he added.

Article Title: ‘We have made our mark, but do we have any support yet?’: Quimcy D’Souza’s fight to put Indian teqball on the map
Article Text:
Quimcy D’Souza (AP/PTI)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: When Quimcy D’Souza first picked up a teqball ball in August 2022, she had no coach, no established training system and little idea of how far the sport could take her. A footballer already, she had discovered teqball after watching a reel of Brazilian football legend Ronaldinho. What began as curiosity quickly turned into something much bigger.“I managed to put the ball back on the first goal. I think that clicked everything for me,” she recalls.Within two months, D’Souza had competed at the national championships and won. Four years later, she is a seven-time national champion, has competed in more than a dozen international tournaments and has established herself among India’s leading teqball players.Her fourth-place finish at the Asian Games in Japan in 2026 has helped introduce the sport to a wider Indian audience. Yet, for D’Souza, the achievement comes with a difficult question: how further could Indian teqball go if its athletes did not have to fight for financial support alongside their opponents?“I started playing in 2022, and nobody followed the sport. Nobody knew who Quimcy was, nobody knew what teqball was,” she says.“Today, after my first two matches and when I made it to the semifinals at this year’s Asian Games the internet actually boomed. People started knowing what teqball was.”For a sport that combines footballing technique with the precision of table tennis, the sudden attention has been significant. D’Souza believes that even getting more people to recognise the sport is an achievement in itself.Sport was never an afterthought for D’Souza. Growing up watching her father play football, she inherited a passion that eventually became a personal mission.“He always dreamt one day to play for India, and I wanted to kind of fulfil it,” she says.Her sporting journey began on the athletics track. Competing for Maharashtra, she ran the 1,500m and 3,000m at the national level. She later took up competitive football, representing Maharashtra at the Under-19 level.An ACL tear, however, forced her to reconsider her playing career. At a time when access to rehabilitation and sports medicine was more limited, continuing football became difficult. Rather than leave sport behind, she chose to study sports management, hoping to contribute to the industry beyond the field.She worked with Decathlon while continuing to explore opportunities in sport. Teqball arrived during this period, opening a new competitive avenue.In 2023, D’Souza moved to Bengaluru with her colleague Chelsea, with whom she founded Teqball Club of Bangalore. At the time, Maharashtra and Gujarat were the sport’s dominant centres in India, with relatively few players competing across other states.The move was about more than pursuing her own ambitions. It was an attempt to build something that could outlast her individual career.The club went on to develop national-level players, including three athletes under the age of 16 who progressed to represent India at the Asian Youth Games in Bahrain. All three subsequently became national champions.For D’Souza, that development is among the most rewarding parts of her journey. Some young players have even moved away from football to concentrate on teqball, while parents have shown an encouraging willingness to prioritise their children's sporting ambitions.The challenge now is to turn that enthusiasm into a wider movement.D’Souza’s progress has come at a considerable personal cost.Without a coach to guide her, she learnt by watching videos, studying other players and recording international opponents to analyse their techniques later. She saved money to compete abroad, treating each tournament as both a competition and an opportunity to learn.“I’m 24 now. I started when I was 21. From 21 up until 24, all my savings have been teqball,” she says.In four years, she has competed in 12 international tours, funding the trips herself. Her father supported her ambitions, but family circumstances made it important for her to become financially independent.The international exposure was crucial. Her performances and world ranking helped her meet the selection criteria for the Asian Games, which required players to be among Asia’s top eight.Without the money to travel, compete and gain ranking points, the Asian Games opportunity might never have materialised.What makes her story particularly striking is that the situation has barely changed despite the breakthrough.“Just to answer your very last question in short, it is the same even now,” she says when asked whether funding has improved.D’Souza says the sport's governing structure in India is yet to secure the necessary recognition from the Sports Authority of India or the sports ministry. Without that institutional backing, athletes continue to shoulder the cost of competing internationally.With world championships approaching, the uncertainty remains.“We’ve made our mark, but do we have any support yet? No, because we’re still thinking about how to save money,” she says.It is a sobering reality for an athlete who has already demonstrated that Indian players can compete with established international opponents.The Asian Games exposed both the potential of Indian teqball and the distance the country still has to travel.D’Souza identifies Thailand as a major force in the sport, while pointing to the strength of the Asian competition more broadly. She was particularly struck by Myanmar and Indonesia, whose players, she says, had received substantial govt support and access to international coaches in the lead-up to the Games.Their preparation offered a glimpse of what sustained investment can achieve.For athletes balancing employment, training, travel arrangements and tournament preparation, such support can make an enormous difference.D’Souza’s own routine involves strength training two or three times a week and table sessions four days a week, including drills, technical work and match practice. As a major tournament approaches, she reduces gym work to concentrate on table training.But training is only one part of the equation. An athlete who must also arrange funding, plan international travel and work without a dedicated coach is carrying responsibilities that have little to do with performance.Indian teqball has nevertheless expanded beyond its original strongholds. D’Souza says around 15 states now compete at the national level, compared with the handful that dominated when she began in 2022.The Asian Games exposure, she hopes, will encourage more states to enter the sport and give young players a reason to take it seriously.D’Souza’s message to potential sponsors is direct: Indian teqball has already shown what it can do without a support system.“We have reached a level like this, where we are top four in Asia and in the top 30s in the world,” she says. “If we can do this by ourselves without any support, I think with support, we will only get better.”She is not asking for recognition based on potential alone. The results are already there, along with a growing player base and a club that is producing national champions.What remains missing is the structure that allows athletes to concentrate on becoming better rather than constantly wondering how they will afford the next tournament.For D’Souza, the Asian Games were proof that India belongs in the conversation. The next step is ensuring that the achievement becomes a beginning rather than a one-off moment of attention.Her journey began with a reel of Ronaldinho and a ball that bounced back onto a curved table. It has since taken her to international competitions, national titles and the brink of a breakthrough for Indian teqball.Now, she wants the country to look beyond the novelty of the sport and recognise the athletes building its future.The message is simple: India has shown it can compete. NEW DELHI: India batter Tilak Varma was involved in an unusual run-out during the third T20I against West Indies on Sunday after a misunderstanding with Axar Patel cost him his wicket.The incident took place in the 17th over, with Gudakesh Motie bowling to Axar. The Indian all-rounder flicked a low full toss towards deep backward square leg, where Kamil Pooran dived to prevent the ball from reaching the boundary.Tilak and Axar seemed convinced that Pooran had touched the boundary rope while attempting the save. Assuming that the ball would be called a four, the two batters completed a single before exchanging a fist bump in the middle of the pitch.However, Pooran had managed to stop the ball just before it reached the boundary and quickly returned it to the field.Axar, who was facing the delivery, realised the situation and grounded his bat at the non-striker's end just in time. Tilak, meanwhile, continued walking towards his crease, unaware that the ball was still in play.Motie collected the ball and broke the stumps at the bowler's end. The third umpire reviewed the incident, first confirming that Pooran had made a clean save before ruling Tilak run out.Tilak departed after scoring 28 off 16 balls, including four fours, as India's lack of awareness led to an unusual dismissal.Despite losing Tilak in the closing stages, India posted 223 in their 20 overs. Abhishek Sharma provided the biggest contribution with a 30-ball 69, including five sixes.Abhishek and Ishan Kishan put on 108 runs off just 40 balls. Kishan scored 37 off 18 deliveries before Roston Chase stumped him. Chase also dismissed India captain Shreyas Iyer lbw for one.The two wickets triggered a mini-collapse, with India losing four wickets for 20 runs to slip to 135/5.West Indies had chased down a target of 250 in the second T20I, but India bounced back in the third match to win by 14 runs and take a 2-1 lead in the five-match series.Arshdeep Singh picked up three wickets for 44 runs, while Naman Dhir claimed two for 39 as West Indies finished on 209/7.Pooran scored 42 and Shimron Hetmyer made 43, adding 60 runs for the second wicket. Dhir dismissed both batters to put India back in control during the middle overs.Sherfane Rutherford scored 32 off 20 balls, while Shamar Springer remained unbeaten on 35 off just 11 deliveries. Springer struck three sixes in the final over against Axar Patel, but West Indies fell short of the target.After the match, India captain Shreyas Iyer praised the confidence shown by his bowlers."It was wonderful to see the bowlers being confident," India captain Shreyas Iyer said after the game. "The clarity was very much visible when I was interacting. They were ready to take up the challenge, and that's what we want."India had won the series opener by eight wickets in Lucknow before West Indies levelled the contest with a six-wicket victory in Ranchi. Sunday's win put India back in front at 2-1.The fourth T20I will be played in Hyderabad on Wednesday.

Article Title: 'Remain ruthless': Abhishek Sharma reveals Team India's huddle talk during West Indies thriller
Article Text:
Abhishek Sharma (AFP Photo)

Abhishek reveals what India discussed in the huddle

Springer's attack keeps India on their toes

NEW DELHI: Team India did not want to give West Indies any chance to fight back in the third T20I in Indore. Abhishek Sharma revealed that the team discussed staying ruthless in the huddle as the hosts defended their total in Indore on Sunday.India secured a 14-run victory to take a 2-1 lead in the five-match series. After scoring 223, the hosts restricted West Indies to 209/7, with Arshdeep Singh taking three wickets and Naman Dhir claiming two.However, West Indies kept the pressure on India until the final over. Shamar Springer smashed an unbeaten 35 off just 11 balls, including three sixes and a boundary, but could not take his team over the line.Abhishek, who led India's batting with 69 off 30 deliveries, spoke about the team's approach during the post-match press conference.Abhishek said India knew West Indies had the ability to turn a match around quickly. The team had witnessed this in the previous game and wanted to avoid giving the visitors another opportunity to stage a comeback.“I think the West Indies is the kind of team against whom you can never say that the match has swung completely in our favor. That was in our minds, because we saw in the last match as well that whichever batter walks in, given the conditions here, it's very easy for them to take the game away from anywhere.So that was in our minds; even when wickets were falling, the talk in the huddle was that we need to remain ruthless from here on, not let them off the hook, and not give them even a single chance to make a comeback,” he said.Springer's late hitting showed why India were determined to stay focused rather than assume the match was already won.Springer made India's task difficult with his aggressive batting towards the end of the chase. Abhishek admitted he was surprised by some of the shots the West Indies batter played and stressed the importance of executing plans under pressure.“If you saw today, the way Springer batted, I got really surprised by the way he played those shots; they weren't easy shots. In that case, you have to be on your toes all the time. Even if they are 50 for 5, they have the capability to turn things around. We were very much prepared this time that we had to be ruthless. Even if we had a good powerplay with the ball, we couldn't afford to give them even one bad ball. We just wanted to execute our plans, and that's what we did,” he said.India's bowlers managed to defend the total despite Springer's late assault. The victory put the hosts ahead in the series, with the fourth T20I scheduled to take place in Hyderabad on Wednesday.Abhishek also achieved a significant milestone during his innings in Indore. He became the fastest batter to score 2,000 runs in men's T20I cricket in terms of balls faced, reaching the mark in 1,024 deliveries.He broke the previous record held by former India T20I captain Suryakumar Yadav, who had taken 1,164 balls to reach 2,000 runs. Former Australia captain Aaron Finch is third on the list, having needed 1,283 deliveries.Abhishek's record-breaking effort helped India put up a challenging total and eventually secure an important win in the five-match series.
Article Summary: India secured a 14-run victory to take a 2-1 lead in the five-match series. Abhishek Sharma became the fastest batter to score 2,000 runs in men's T20I cricket in terms of balls faced. He broke the previous record held by former India captain Suryakumar Yadav.
